newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia's Packer looks ready to pounce.
newsitem.headline: Australia's Packer looks ready to pounce.

text.p: Kerry Packer appears to be the verge of another major acquisition, possibly worth up to A$5.0 billion (US$3.95 billion), after selling most of his stake in casino operator Crown Casino Ltd, analysts said.
The question is, what will be his target?
Australia's richest man has interests in television, magazines, advertising inserts, telecommunications, chemicals, casinos, beef and cotton farms.

The media-shy billionaire also has a tendency to turn up in unexpected places, such as on the share register of banks and engineering groups at a time when their share prices are languishing at cyclically low levels, analysts said.
The rumoured targets this time include newspaper group John Fairfax Holdings Ltd, or possibly U.S. casino operator Showboat Inc, the operator of the Sydney Harbour Casino.
But nobody really knows for sure.

The polo-playing businessman has an estimated personal fortune of A$3.3 billion. He also has a a A$2.0 billion bank credit facility which he has hardly used and the capacity to borrow more or raise equity financing through his listed Publishing and Broadcasting Ltd
Packer companies have raised about A$330 million over the last three months from reducing stakes in Crown and Fairfax and the sale of an eight percent stake in cinema group Village Roadshow Ltd

The local bourse is bracing itself for a Packer move after a rare statement made on Tuesday by his private company, Consolidated Press Holdings Ltd (CPH), when it sold 75 million Crown shares to raise A$204 million.
"CPH's sale was motivated by the wish to liquefy some of its assets for use in other transactions and in no way reflects on CPH's confidence in Crown," CPH said.
The market latched on to the phrase "other transactions".
"He has got such a range of interests that you could never really guess what it might be," said Lachlan Drummond, a media analyst at brokers First Pacific Stockbrokers.
The only business Packer has clearly stated he wants to acquire is Fairfax, Australia's oldest newspaper group.
He is prevented from taking control of the company by cross-media ownerhip rules which prevent a television operator from controlling a major newspaper in the same market.
In August, Packer reduced his Fairfax stake to 15 percent from just over 17 and at the same time sold the Fairfax shares held by CPH to his Publishing and Broadcasting (PBL) subsidiary.
The same day PBL said the preferred outcome of the group's stake in Fairfax was a merger between the PBL and Fairfax.
But media analysts ruled out a move by Packer on Fairfax, which is controlled by Canadian media baron Conrad Black.

"Packer is not known for telegraphing what he is going to do and cashing up and moving on Fairfax would not be a subtle move, as the whole market is watching Fairfax. So maybe he might do something else," said ANZ Securities media analyst Bob Peters.

The market is also waiting to see if PBL exercises its option to increase its stake in pay television and telephone group Optus Vision to 20 percent from a current five percent. That would cost about A$200 million.
Analysts said Packer has not given any signals on whether he intends to take up the option, due to expire in November 1997.
But Packer has a knack for surprising the market.

The market has not forgotten that he joined forces with fellow billionaire Sir James Goldsmith in 1989 in an unsuccessful tilt at British conglomerate B.A.T Industries Plc. That bid was worth 13 billion stg -- about A$26 billion at today's exchange rates.
